questions.text: What is your vision for safe streets in Jersey City and what will you do to achieve it?
What modes of transportation will you prioritize in Jersey City?
In Jersey City currently, the Department of Infrastructure budget is $3 million. Would you increase or decrease this budget and why?

In Jersey City currently, the Department of Public Safety budget is $214 million. Would you increase or decrease this budget and why? How would you ensure adequate traffic enforcement by our police department?

Do you support redesigning streets to include protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and safer crosswalks? If so, which streets or corridors would you prioritize first? Please name at least three in your ward / citywide?

Over $8.1 million in federal funds has been approved for safety improvements on Summit Avenue from Route 139 to Secaucus Road. Do you support the Baldwin and Summit one-way pairing to make room for protected bike lanes?
What strategies would you implement to protect pedestrian spaces and ensure people on e-bikes and other micro-mobility devices do not ride on sidewalks?

The Newark Avenue Pedestrian Plaza has become a vital hub for local businesses and a popular public space for residents, families, and visitors. Do you support the continued expansion and permanency of this plaza?

Beyond Newark Avenue, do you support the creation of new pedestrian-only spaces or the expansion of existing ones throughout the city? Please identify at least one specific area in Jersey City where you believe a new pedestrian plaza or shared street would be most beneficial and explain your rationale.
Do you support bus rapid transit? If so, on which corridors? Are you willing to remove parking to speed up buses?
Please select one of these streets you would like to target for safety improvements. Council candidates, please select a street in your ward.
What specific changes do you propose to make the street listed in Q11 safer?
Will you commit to voting for these changes within 24 months of taking office?

Please review the included map from the Bike Master Plan that was unanimously approved by city council in 2019. Six years later this plan is still incomplete. Pick one or more streets that you support installing a protected bike lane? Council candidates, please select a street in your ward.
Will you commit to voting for these changes within 24 months of taking office?

There is no such thing as free parking. Street parking disadvantages residents without access to a motor vehicle and increased congestion for those who do. Are you willing to reduce car parking to reallocate street space for other modes, such as pedestrians, bicyclists, and dedicated bus lanes? Have you advocated for these projects in the past? Be specific.
Are you willing to continue Mayor Fulop’s commitment to Vision Zero? What would you do differently?

Over the past several years, our city has invested significant public funds and political capital in implementing active transportation infrastructure, such as protected bike lanes and enhanced crosswalks. These projects were installed to improve public safety, support local businesses, and move the city closer to its Vision Zero goals. What is your position on proposals to remove or alter previously installed safe streets infrastructure, and what specific criteria or data would you use to evaluate and decide on the permanence of these public assets?
Provide an idea for a public education campaign on the topic of safe streets.
How do you integrate the need for community engagement along with the need to implement these lifesaving safety measures?

What community engagement strategies do you see as most effective? Are you willing to stand up for lifesaving improvements or do you see yourself as a neutral participant? What examples do you have of community engagement/education for your policies?

What will you do to ensure children have safe routes to walk or bike to school? Which schools do you think are candidates for “slow streets” or “school streets”--streets that are closed to vehicles during school hours or permanently?
How do you see safe streets fitting into broader goals like climate action, cleaner air, and public health?
When getting around Jersey City what are your top modes of transportation.
Please explain your answer to the previous question
Are you willing to take the Vision Zero pledge?
questions.extra:
I, a resident and candidate for public office in Jersey City, hereby take the Vision Zero pledge. I commit to making traffic safety my top priority and acknowledge that every traffic-related death and serious injury is preventable. As a road user, I pledge to:

  1. Prioritize Safety: I will always put the safety of others first, whether I am cycling, driving, or walking. I will be mindful of the most vulnerable road users, including pedestrians, children, seniors, and people with disabilities, and will yield to them in accordance with the rules of the road.
  2. Drive Distraction-Free: I will not use a mobile device while driving, and I will maintain my full attention on the road and my surroundings at all times to ensure a safe journey for everyone.
  3. Obey All Traffic Laws: I will operate my vehicle at safe speeds, obey all traffic signals and signs, and come to a complete stop at all red lights and stop signs.

questions.text: Have you or someone you know been a victim of traffic violence? How does this impact your view of policy?

Do you support removing mandatory parking requirements in new housing? How do you address the criticism that mandatory parking requirements raise the monthly rent of new housing by about $500 per unit of parking?
Do you support strengthening bicycle parking requirements in new housing, including parking for cargo bikes and ebikes, to enable more carfree households?

According to the American Community Survey, in 2023 41% of households in Jersey City were car free. Given the development that has already been approved for Jersey City, how will you address the transit needs of these new residents? If at the end of your term of office, if that number has not changed or gone down will you see that as a policy failure?
Do you support the expansion of the New Jersey Turnpike in Jersey City?

In New York City, 1,800 automated speed cameras reduced crashes by 14% and decreased speeding by 75%. Automated speed enforcement is currently banned at the statewide level in New Jersey. Do you support reversing this ban? Would you support installing automated enforcement mechanisms in Jersey City?

What levers of changing policy for improving street safety will you utilize if elected to your position, and how will you work with other levels of government, including county and state, to holistically improve the regional transit system?

responses:
My vision for safe streets in Jersey City is centered on children’s safety first and making our neighborhoods more walkable, accessible, and community-focused. I will achieve this through a comprehensive approach:

Zero tolerance in school and park zones with a 15 MPH speed limit, safe drop-off rules, and enforcement against blocked walkways.
Raised crosswalks and permanent curb bump-outs to slow traffic and give pedestrians priority.

No Right Turn on Red citywide, pushed-back stop lines, and stronger pedestrian right-of-way laws to reduce crashes.

Education + enforcement: working with JCPD and schools to instill safe habits, enforce the “No Touch” law, and hold drivers accountable.

Better signage and infrastructure like “Children at Play” and “School Zone” signs, helmet/bike gear requirements, and safe e-bike/moped regulation.

I will prioritize walking, biking, and public transit because they keep our city accessible, affordable, and environmentally sustainable. Cars will remain part of our city, but my focus is on pedestrian-first design, protected bike lanes, reliable buses, and safe micro-mobility (e-bikes, scooters, mopeds). By investing in these modes, we reduce congestion, improve air quality, and make streets safer for everyone.

I would increase the Department of Infrastructure budget because $3 million is not enough for a city of our size and growth. The infrastruture is outdated. 

Expanding this budget would allow:

Input raised crosswalks and curb bump-outs

Upgraded sidewalks and stormwater drainage (critical after heavy rains)

Stronger bike infrastructure and signage

These investments save lives, reduce long-term maintenance costs, and strengthen the backbone of our community.

I would reallocate within the current $214 million budget rather than broadly increase it. Public safety should focus not only on crime but also on traffic safety, pedestrian protection, and quality of life enforcement. I will:

Dedicate traffic enforcement units in school and park zones

Partner JCPD with schools for traffic safety education

Use technology like red-light and speed cameras to assist enforcement and free up officers for priority calls

Ensure transparency in how resources are allocated, so that enforcement is consistent and equitable across all neighborhoods

Yes, I fully support redesigning our streets with protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and safer crosswalks. The first corridors I would prioritize are:

Summit Avenue (citywide corridor) – already receiving federal funding, but should include stronger pedestrian protections.

Communipaw Avenue & Ocean Avenue (Ward A/F) – busy corridors with schools and parks where safer crosswalks and bike lanes will save lives.
Yes, I support the Baldwin and Summit one-way pairing to make room for protected bike lanes—as long as it’s done with community input and equity in mind.

I will enforce a “Pedestrian-Only Means Pedestrian-Only” policy for sidewalks and plazas. My strategies include:

Dedicated protected bike and micro-mobility lanes so riders have safe alternatives to sidewalks.

Clear signage and pavement markings remind riders that sidewalks are for walking only.
Speed and licensing rules: riders over 20mph must have a driver’s license, and all e-bike/moped riders must obey traffic laws.

JCPD + community enforcement: targeted patrols in high-traffic pedestrian zones, plus ticketing for violations.

Education campaigns in schools and community centers to build safe riding habits from an early age.

Yes, I support making the Newark Avenue Pedestrian Plaza permanent and expanding it thoughtfully. The plaza has proven that safe, people-first streets increase foot traffic, boost local businesses, and create a stronger sense of community. My administration will work with local businesses and residents to ensure expansion benefits everyone—providing accessibility, safety, and family-friendly design.

Yes, I support creating more pedestrian-only and shared public spaces across Jersey City. One area I would prioritize is Martin Luther King Drive near Bethune Center and the Greenville Library.

This corridor has high foot traffic, schools, businesses, and cultural institutions.
A pedestrian plaza or shared street here would provide a safe gathering space, support small businesses, and celebrate the cultural identity of the neighborhood.

Other potential areas include Bergen Avenue near Journal Square and West Side Avenue by Lincoln Park, where plazas would bring more walkability, safety, and community activity.

Yes, I support Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) as part of a cleaner, faster, and more affordable transit system for Jersey City. The corridors I would prioritize are:

Summit Avenue (a primary north-south connector already slated for federal safety funding).

Montgomery Street / Communipaw Avenue linking Greenville to Journal Square and Downtown.

West Side Avenue serves residential neighborhoods and connects to key parks and schools.

I am willing to reallocate some curbside parking to make BRT work—because moving thousands of people safely and efficiently outweighs the benefit of a few car storage spaces. However, I would pair these changes with residential parking solutions and partnerships with local garages so residents and businesses are not unfairly burdened.
A, B,

I would prioritize Martin Luther King Drive, Summit Avenue, and Communipaw Avenue for immediate safety improvements. These corridors have some of the highest pedestrian activity in the city, with schools, parks, businesses, and transit connections. 

Raised crosswalks, protected bike lanes, permanent curb bump-outs, and clear signage can reduce crashes and keep children and families safe.
Yes

I support installing protected bike lanes on calmer corridors and neighborhood connectors rather than the busiest, high-traffic streets. My priority is to create a network that allows children, families, and everyday riders to move safely through Jersey City without being placed in conflict with heavy car traffic.

Streets like Garfield Avenue, Clendenny Avenue, and Duncan Avenue are strong candidates for protected bike lanes because they run through residential and school areas where safety is most critical. I also support completing connections along Sip Avenue and Montgomery Street near parks and schools.

In high-traffic corridors like Summit Avenue, MLK Drive, and Communipaw Avenue, I believe the focus should instead be on pedestrian protections (raised crosswalks, curb bump-outs, 15 MPH school zones, and stricter enforcement)rather than inserting bike lanes that could compromise safety or add congestion.
Yes

I am not in favor of reducing street parking to reallocate space. Parking in Jersey City is already limited, and many working families, seniors, and residents with disabilities depend on their cars for daily life. Taking away parking would create unnecessary hardships and increase tensions in neighborhoods that are already struggling with congestion.

Instead, I believe in improving safety and mobility through better design and enforcement without reducing parking. This includes:

Raised crosswalks, permanent curb bump-outs, and better signage in school and park zones.

Dedicated bus rapid transit lanes on existing wide corridors where space allows, paired with smart traffic light management.

Expanding off-street parking partnerships with garages and lots so residents and visitors have more options without losing curbside spaces.

My advocacy has consistently been about balancing safety with fairness. I support making streets safer for pedestrians, bicyclists, and bus riders — but not at the expense of residents who need access to reliable parking in their neighborhoods.

I support the goals of Vision Zero because no loss of life on our streets is acceptable. 

However, Jersey City needs a smarter and more community-focused approach than what has been done so far.

Where I would do things differently:

Zero Tolerance School & Park Zones – Enforce a 15 MPH speed limit, safe drop-offs, and no commercial vehicles blocking walkways around schools and playgrounds.

Focus on education + enforcement – Partner with JCPD, schools, and community organizations to teach safe habits and enforce laws like “No Right on Red” and “No Touch” in a fair and consistent way.

Prioritize raised crosswalks and curb bump-outs – Physical design changes naturally slow cars and protect children without relying solely on tickets.

Target the right streets – Focus improvements on residential, school, and park-adjacent streets where children and families walk every day, not already congested major corridors.
Transparency and accountability – Publish clear, regular reports on crashes, enforcement, and progress so residents can measure real results.

Mayor Fulop’s Vision Zero was heavy on promises but light on community accountability. We are all responsible for safety in our city. I will keep the commitment to safer streets, but I will deliver results that residents can actually see and feel in their neighborhoods.

I believe that safe streets infrastructure should be preserved and improved when it is working, but re-evaluated when it is not meeting community needs. Public safety is always the priority, but we must balance it with fairness, accessibility, and transparency.

My position is:

Keep what’s working: 

If a protected bike lane or crosswalk has reduced crashes, improved safety for children and seniors, and supported local businesses, it should stay.

Re-evaluate what’s not working: If a project has increased congestion, harmed small businesses, or created confusion for drivers and pedestrians, it should be reviewed with real community input.

Specific criteria I would use include:

Crash and injury data before and after installation
Traffic flow and emergency vehicle access
Business feedback and economic impact
Community surveys and school zone safety reports
Pedestrian and cyclist usage data

I will not support removing safety infrastructure just because it is unpopular or politically inconvenient. But I will insist that it is effective, equitable, and accountable — and that residents are part of the decision-making process from start to finish.

I would launch the “Walk. Ride. Drive. JC Safely” education campaign. This initiative would partner with schools, community organizations, and local businesses to host safety events, install bold signage, and showcase student-designed safety signs throughout the city.
I would host community forums, school partnerships, and free citywide trainings on safety and how to provide first aid to someone who may be injured.

I believe the most effective community engagement strategies are meeting people where they are—in schools, churches, parks, senior centers, and neighborhood associations—so residents feel heard and respected. I am willing to stand up for lifesaving improvements. Outside of being a police officer, I volunteer my time to mentor youth, host community playdates, and create children’s coloring and reading books that teach important lessons in fun and accessible ways. My efforts reflect my belief that education, transparency, and collaboration are the best ways to engage residents and build trust.

I will ensure children have safe routes to walk or bike to school by focusing on traffic calming, raised crosswalks, 15 MPH school zones, curb bump-outs, and strict enforcement around schools rather than closing streets and creating more congestion. I am not interested in closing streets, as this does not solve the root issue. The real problem is the sheer number of cars that pass through Jersey City daily, and we must address that directly. I support strategies to recoup funds from non-resident vehicles traveling through the city and reinvest those dollars into infrastructure improvements and safety measures—ensuring schools have the resources they need to keep children safe without burdening local residents.

Safe streets are directly connected to climate action, cleaner air, and public health. I am aware of the pollution hot spots in Jersey City, and we can combat them by providing reliable transportation alternatives that reduce car dependency. My vision includes creating a Jersey City Electric Bus Line to cut traffic emissions, while also expanding opportunities for biking, scooters, and other micro-mobility options. Reliable transit means less reliance on cars, cleaner air for our children, and healthier communities across the city.

1. I Drive Myself
2. Walking
3. Driven by others (taxi, ride-share, etc)

Not selected: Bike, Bus, PATH/HBLR/Ferry

I live and work in Jersey City as a police officer, and my vehicle is an essential part of getting back and forth through the city. At the same time, I prefer to walk in my leisure time, as it helps me decompress and stay connected to the community. I also use rideshare services, as driving is a requirement of my work duties, and rideshare gives me a break from driving.
Yes

Yes, I have encountered traffic violence in my work as a police officer. These tragedies are often preventable—whether by practicing situational awareness, slowing down, or simply taking a few extra moments before proceeding. This experience has shaped my belief that policy must focus on both infrastructure improvements and education so that drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians all share responsibility for keeping our streets safe

I support re-evaluating mandatory parking requirements in new housing, especially in areas well served by transit. Parking construction drives up the cost of housing—sometimes by $500 or more per unit—and that burden falls on renters and families who may not even own a car. Instead of blanket requirements, I support a flexible, context-based approach: in transit-rich areas, developers should be allowed to build less parking and pass the savings on to residents, while in other neighborhoods, we should balance parking needs with affordability. My priority is ensuring that housing remains accessible and affordable, while investing in better transit and safer streets so more people feel comfortable not relying on their.

Yes, I support strengthening bicycle parking requirements in new housing, including secure space for cargo bikes and e-bikes. As more families and residents choose car-free or low-car lifestyles, housing design should reflect those needs.

I support creating a toll system for out-of-state and out-of-city drivers so they contribute to our infrastructure and safety improvements. I also propose a Jersey City Electric Bus Line to provide clean, reliable transit and reduce car reliance. If the percentage of car-free households does not grow by the end of my term, I would view that as a policy failure.

I do not support the expansion of the New Jersey Turnpike in Jersey City. The proposed plan would worsen environmental injustice in neighborhoods that are already hot spots for pollution and disproportionately impacted by respiratory diseases and cardiovascular issues. Instead of expanding highways, we should invest in clean transit and infrastructure improvements that improve public health and quality of life.

I do not support reversing the statewide ban on automated speed enforcement in New Jersey. These cameras were banned because of widespread concerns about fairness, reliability, and revenue-driven enforcement, where tickets often became more about generating money than improving safety. Instead, I recommend alternatives that focus on equity and accountability: expanding the use of raised crosswalks, permanent curb bump-outs, and traffic-calming design that naturally slows vehicles, along with targeted JCPD enforcement in school and park zones. These solutions prioritize safety without creating a system that unfairly burdens residents.

If elected, I will use every lever available to improve street safety, starting with city ordinances, budget priorities, and enforcement policies that create safer conditions around schools, parks, and busy pedestrian areas. I will prioritize raised crosswalks, permanent curb bump-outs, school zone speed limits, and stricter enforcement of “No Right on Red.”
At the county and state level, I will advocate for increased transit funding, regional electric bus service, and investments in cleaner air infrastructure, while opposing projects like the NJ Turnpike expansion, which worsen environmental and safety conditions. I will also work with state partners to explore alternatives to automated enforcement, such as design-based traffic calming and fairer, community-driven approaches to safety.
Holistic improvements require collaboration, and I will ensure Jersey City has a strong voice in shaping a regional transit system that reduces car dependency, addresses congestion, and creates safer, healthier neighborhoods.

I would keep the overall Department of Public Safety budget steady and fix how it is managed. School safety comes first. I will set clear safeguards on overtime with monthly public reporting, stabilize pay and scheduling for crossing guards, and build a reliable substitute pool so police officers are not pulled from core law enforcement to cover school posts. Traffic enforcement will focus on the most dangerous behaviors and crash hot spots during school hours, coordinated with Infrastructure on engineering near schools. If state law allows modern tools in the future, I will evaluate them with due process protections.

I will prioritize walking and public transit, support a more connected bike network as the city continues to invest, and keep driving safe and predictable. In the Heights, I will work with the city, the county, and NJ Transit to improve bus reliability and expand micro-transit so neighbors in the steep hill area have practical access to transit, with curb management that supports merchants, deliveries, and disability access.

I would support a targeted increase focused on maintenance and quick build safety projects, while using federal and county funds first. Any local adjustment should come with clear project lists, delivery timelines, and public scorecards so residents can track results and we can adjust based on performance.

I would hold the budget steady and direct traffic enforcement to the behaviors and locations that cause the most harm, coordinated with engineering fixes that prevent crashes. I will pair education on New Jersey’s Safe Passing Law with data informed deployments and transparent reporting, and I will support modern tools only where they comply with state law and protect civil rights.

Yes. I support redesigns that include protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and safer crosswalks where the data and context support them, with curb management for loading, ADA access, and emergency response. I will prioritize corridors already identified or funded in public programs, including the Summit Avenue corridor, Palisade Avenue near schools, and Central Avenue in the business district for safer crossings and orderly loading. Final design and phasing will follow inclusive outreach in English and Spanish, with translation available in other languages commonly spoken in the ward, a published equity assessment, and public safety and access metrics, using quick build pilots where helpful.

I support delivering the Summit Avenue safety project, including a protected facility. Before selecting a final design, I will complete inclusive outreach in English and Spanish, with translation available in other languages commonly spoken in the area, and publish an equity assessment focused on safety, access, and emergency response. If the one way pairing proves to deliver the best results, I would advance a time limited pilot with published metrics for injuries, bus reliability, emergency response times, and access for seniors, people with disabilities, and small businesses. We will keep what works, fix what does not, and make the final design decision on the data.

I will pair design, education, and enforcement. Design means clearer markings, protected facilities where data supports them, “dismount” zones in the most crowded areas, and secure parking and loading so riders have safe alternatives to the sidewalk. Education will use the city’s PedalSmart materials and multilingual outreach for delivery workers and riders. Enforcement will be targeted in school zones and business districts, focusing on the most dangerous behavior and repeat violations, consistent with city rules that keep bikes and micromobility off sidewalks in business areas.

I support Newark Avenue’s plaza as a city asset, with continued operation tied to a clear management plan for sanitation, ADA access, emergency access, loading, and public safety. Because it is outside my ward, I will respect the district member’s lead and the community process there. For any expansion or permanence, I support a transparent plan, published metrics, and active engagement with nearby residents and merchants before final decisions.

Yes, where the context and data support it. I would begin with time-limited “School Streets” that close a short block directly fronting a school during arrival and dismissal, and a weekend shared-street pilot on a side street off the Central Avenue business district. Both would maintain emergency access, include a loading plan for merchants, and proceed only after inclusive, multilingual outreach and a published evaluation of safety and economic outcomes.

Yes. I support bus-priority and BRT elements on corridors with the highest ridership and delay, including the county’s ongoing work to study JFK Boulevard. I am willing to remove parking only where data show significant gains in bus speed and reliability and where loading, ADA access, and nearby parking alternatives are addressed through a management plan. I would start with quick-build pilots, signal priority, and transparent performance metrics, then make permanent changes if the results hold.
D

On Summit Avenue and Central Avenue, I will start with quick build safety improvements at high injury and school areas, including daylighting, high visibility crosswalks, leading pedestrian intervals, corner tightening, and signal upgrades. Where the crash data and street context support it, I will add protected facilities and pair them with a curb management plan that preserves ADA access, deliveries, and reliable emergency response. I will also improve bus reliability where appropriate through signal priority and safer access to stops. All design steps will follow inclusive outreach in English and Spanish, with translation available in other languages commonly spoken in the ward, and a published equity and access review. Permanent elements will follow a time limited pilot and a public evaluation of safety, access, and operations. For Jersey Avenue, which is outside Ward D, I will coordinate with the district member to apply the same process and metrics.

I will vote within 24 months to initiate a time limited pilot on the selected corridors and to publish a public evaluation with metrics for injuries and severe injuries, transit reliability, emergency response, ADA access, and loading. I will vote to make any design permanent only if the pilot meets the published targets and passes the equity, language access, and emergency access review.

I support installing a protected bike lane on Palisade Avenue as identified in the Bike Master Plan, delivered first as a time limited pilot with a curb management plan for ADA access, deliveries, and emergency response. On Summit Avenue, I will evaluate protected or separated options and begin with quick build safety improvements, selecting the final configuration after engineering review, inclusive outreach in English and Spanish with translation in other local languages, and a funding plan that uses federal, county, and state sources before local dollars.

Yes. I will vote within 24 months to initiate the pilot and to publish a public evaluation with metrics for injuries and severe injuries, transit reliability where relevant, emergency response, ADA access, and loading. I will vote to make any design permanent only after those results meet the published targets, outreach and equity steps are complete, and dedicated funding is in place without cutting essential services.

I know many Ward D residents rely on a car for work, medical care, and caregiving. I will consider reallocating limited parking space when the safety data show meaningful benefits for people walking, biking, and buses, and when a curb-management plan protects ADA access, deliveries, school operations, and emergency response. I would start with small, time-limited pilots near schools and bus stops, share results publicly, and decide with residents and merchants.

Yes. I will continue the city’s Vision Zero commitment and strengthen it by focusing first on high-injury locations around schools and seniors, adding inclusive outreach in English and Spanish with translation in other local languages, stabilizing crossing-guard staffing and substitute coverage, aligning enforcement with engineering, and publishing simple scorecards so residents can see progress.

I support keeping or improving projects that meet published safety and access targets. I would evaluate any proposal to modify or remove a treatment using clear metrics for injuries and severe injuries, transit reliability where relevant, emergency response times, ADA compliance, loading and merchant operations, and multilingual community feedback. If results meet the targets, we keep or refine; if not, we adjust the design. Removal is a last resort when both safety and access underperform and an alternative can meet the targets.

I would launch “Safe Routes Ward D” in partnership with the Board of Education, school principals, and PTAs. The campaign will include school assemblies and brief classroom lessons delivered with PE and health staff, take-home materials in English and Spanish with translation in other local languages, short videos for families and delivery workers, walking school bus and bike bus pilots, on-street demonstrations near schools, and crossing-guard appreciation and recruitment days. We will measure results through speeds at school fronts, yielding compliance, near-miss reports, and simple student and family travel surveys.

I will run engagement and delivery together. Quick-build fixes at documented high-injury locations move forward while we hold inclusive listening sessions and post the pilot plan and metrics. Residents and merchants help shape designs before anything becomes permanent, and we report results on a simple public dashboard.

The most effective tools are multilingual listening sessions at accessible times, walk-audits near schools and seniors, merchant roundtables on curb needs, and short text or online surveys for those who cannot attend meetings. I will champion life-saving improvements once pilots meet safety and access standards and residents have been heard, and I will use clear timelines and plain-language summaries so people can track decisions.

I will prioritize daylighting, high-visibility crosswalks, leading pedestrian intervals, and safer corners at school fronts, and I will stabilize crossing-guard pay, scheduling, and a substitute pool so officers stay on core assignments. I support short “school street” pilots that close the block directly fronting a school during arrival and dismissal where conditions fit, with emergency access maintained and a clear loading plan. I will work with the Board of Education, school principals, and PTAs to select candidate schools, design short school-street pilots, and share results in English and Spanish with translation in other local languages before any permanent step.

Safe street designs help people make short trips on foot, bike, or transit, which reduces injuries, improves air quality, and supports daily physical activity. I will align projects with transit reliability and, where possible, add shade and street trees so families and seniors have healthy, lower-emission options without losing essential access.

1. I Drive Myself
2. PATH/HBLR/Ferry
3. Walking

Not selected: Bike, Bus, Driven by others

I take the Light Rail to work because it is reliable and reduces congestion. I drive for meetings across the ward and for family obligations outside the city. I walk the ward to meet residents and to see street conditions first hand. Using all three gives me a balanced view of what travelers experience each day.
Yes

Yes. My brother-in-law was struck and killed on Route 440 in Bayonne, and a neighbor on my block in Ward D was injured in a crash near our homes. I worked with residents and city staff to secure a four-way stop at that intersection. These experiences center my approach on preventing severe injuries and deaths through proven design changes, focusing first on school and senior areas, engaging residents in English and Spanish with translation in other local languages, and publishing results so we keep what works and improve what does not.

I support right-sizing or removing mandatory parking minimums near transit and in mixed-use areas when an engineering and mobility analysis shows we can meet access needs with shared and unbundled parking. I do not support a blanket elimination across the city. Research shows that required parking raises development costs and those costs are passed on to renters; the exact amount varies by market. To keep housing more affordable without reducing ADA access or loading, I will require unbundled parking so people without cars are not paying for spaces they do not use, allow shared and off-site parking, and use data to tailor requirements by location. Any changes will be paired with a curb-management plan and will not reduce essential resident services.

Yes. I support stronger bicycle parking requirements that include secure indoor parking and short-term racks, with space and outlets for cargo bikes and e-bikes that meet fire-safety standards. This helps families and workers who choose to live with fewer cars while keeping buildings safe and functional.

I will work with NJ Transit, the county, and the city to improve bus frequency and reliability, expand microtransit where hills limit access, and upgrade shelters, lighting, and real-time information so people can reach jobs, school, and services without a car. I will also make the walk to transit safer with crosswalks, daylighting, and leading pedestrian intervals. I will not judge success by a single statistic. If the share of car-free households does not change, I will still hold us accountable for improving safety outcomes, transit reliability, access to frequent service, and travel times. The goal is practical choices that are safe, affordable, and dependable.

I support necessary safety repairs and modernization of aging Turnpike infrastructure. I do not support adding vehicle capacity that would increase traffic, noise, or pollution in nearby neighborhoods without clear safety, equity, and environmental benefits. Any state project that affects Ward D should include a full impact review, air-quality monitoring, mitigation for neighborhood streets, and investments in transit access and local street safety. I will engage the Turnpike Authority and state partners to protect residents while focusing on practical improvements that keep people safe.

I support giving cities the option to pilot automated speed enforcement with strong safeguards. If the state lifts the ban, I would begin with limited pilots in school zones and on documented high-injury corridors, with clear signage, strict privacy protections, calibrated equipment, due-process rights, fair fine structures, and a requirement that revenue be reinvested in safety near the cameras. We would pair any cameras with engineering fixes and public reporting, and we would continue only if the data show meaningful safety gains.

I will use proven tools and work across agencies. Locally, that means daylighting, high-visibility crosswalks, leading pedestrian intervals, curb-management for ADA access and loading, school-front safety packages, and quick-build pilots with public metrics. I will stabilize crossing-guard staffing and overtime controls so school-hour coverage is reliable. Regionally, I will align ward projects with the Hudson County Vision Zero plan and New Jersey’s Target Zero framework, coordinate with NJ Transit and the county on better bus reliability, and seek federal and state funding so we do not reduce essential services. I will publish simple scorecards so residents can see progress and I will keep designs that meet safety and access targets.

My vision is for Jersey City to be a city where no family fears losing a loved one to unsafe streets, where our streets work for everyone—whether they walk, bike, take transit, or drive. To achieve this, I will:
Continue our Vision Zero plan with clear benchmarks and public accountability.

One of our core platforms is Safe, Clean, Green Streets. This means that every user of our streets, including pedestrians, bicyclists, drivers, transit riders, and people using micromobility options, deserves safe streets.

To achieve this, I will focus on permanent infrastructural interventions in Jersey City. Multiple studies have shown that only lasting infrastructure changes can shift behavior in ways that create safer streets for everyone. We must invest in improvements such as daylighting with amenities, hardened turns, protected bike lanes, and curb extensions that prioritize the safety of our most vulnerable users, especially pedestrians and bicyclists. In addition, we must also implement road dieting and other measures that slow down the speed of vehicles in Jersey City.

We must also put serious pressure on transit agencies, including NJ Transit and the Port Authority, to expand and improve public transit options for our communities. Our buses are constantly late, PATH trains are constantly delayed, and the light rail sometimes straight up disappears on riders. We need to invest in these services and pressure transit authorities to open up new routes and lanes to serve large swaths of our city that are underserviced by public transit, such as in Ward B and Ward D.

I will prioritize green, sustainable mobility options such as public transit, bicycling, walking, and other forms of micromobility. To strengthen public transit, Jersey City should establish a Municipal Transit Council capable of sustaining long-term pressure on NJ Transit and the Port Authority to improve and expand services. This means creating more bus routes, building additional shelters, and installing real-time waiting displays at bus stops. PATH service must also become more frequent during non-peak hours, especially on weekends, to better serve residents traveling to and from the city. For the light rail, it is essential to ensure that NJ Transit’s proposed Hudson-Bergen Light Rail extensions are completed, including the Route 440 station as part of the Bayfront Redevelopment Plan, the Northern Branch project extending service from Tonnelle to Englewood Hospital, and the Passaic-Bergen Extension through Hackensack and Paterson to Hawthorne. These projects would significantly reduce auto commutes into Jersey City and across Hudson County.
At the same time, Jersey City must fully implement its Vision Zero plan for bicycling and walking. This requires sustained infrastructure investments: expanding protected bike lanes, creating a fully connected bike network, and installing pedestrian-friendly features such as leading pedestrian intervals and raised crosswalks. Additional measures like road diets and chicanes can help slow vehicle traffic and make streets safer for everyone.
With the right investments and interventions, we can transform Jersey City into a 15-minute city where residents are never far from their jobs, shopping, healthcare, or entertainment. Everything a person needs should be less than 15 minutes away by walking, biking, or transit. And instead of looking to New York City for inspiration, we should model ourselves on cities like Amsterdam and Paris, where sustainable mobility is already at the core of urban life.

According to Jersey City’s 2024 Vision Zero Annual Report, 55 of the 77 actions (71%) outlined in the Vision Zero Action Plan have been advanced or completed since 2019. Fatal crashes peaked during the pandemic in 2020 and 2021, but dropped to zero in 2023 and have remained below average in the years since. During this period, the city implemented hundreds of speed bumps, new “no turn on red” restrictions, and curb extensions, along with more than 23 miles of bike lanes. Newark Avenue and Bergen Square have undergone major redesigns that both enhanced pedestrian safety and strengthened the character of the neighborhoods. As a result, streets like Bergen Avenue have seen cycling activity more than triple, along with increases in pedestrian traffic and reductions in roadway injuries.
These results make it clear that safe street policies are working. The remaining action items in the Vision Zero plan must be completed, and these safety countermeasures must be expanded to all areas of the city that lack them, including state and county roads, where serious crashes and fatalities remain disproportionately high.

I support town halls, community engagement meetings, and canvassing at local events to educate the public about the benefits of Vision Zero and the infrastructural improvements that make our streets safer. Their recommendations can determine whether a policy for a particular street will be practical and effective in achieving its goals of safety and accessibility for pedestrians, cyclists, and drivers. We should be knocking doors not just during election cycles, but year-round to build more participation and buy-in.
True integration of engagement and policy requires that outreach, communication, and trust start early and remain consistent throughout both the planning and implementation process.

My vision is a Jersey City where no one fears crossing the street or riding a bike in their own neighborhood. I’m committed to a Vision Zero approach – meaning we redesign dangerous streets and intersections, calm down speeding traffic, and hold drivers accountable so that traffic fatalities and serious injuries are eliminated. That means more protected bike lanes, well-marked crosswalks, and pedestrian-friendly design all over the city. As Mayor, I’ll push these improvements aggressively and work hand-in-hand with the community so everyone from kids walking to school to seniors crossing the road can feel safe.

I’ll prioritize walking, biking, and public transit. We need to make it easier to get around without a car, especially since many Jersey City residents rely on walking or transit today. That means better sidewalks and crosswalks for pedestrians, protected lanes for cyclists, and major improvements to our buses and light rail. By focusing on these modes, we can reduce traffic congestion, cut pollution, and ensure everyone has a convenient way to travel around our city, whether or not they own a car.

$3 million is far too low if we’re serious about fixing our streets, so I would seek to increase the Department of Infrastructure’s budget. We have miles of roads to redesign for safety, traffic signals to upgrade, and sidewalks to repair, all of which require more investment. Right now we pour hundreds of millions into other areas, but just a tiny fraction into the infrastructure that could save lives. I’d re-balance our priorities so that more of our tax dollars are invested in Jersey City’s infrastructure of tomorrow, including safer local roads, bike lanes, and transit-friendly streets. Every dollar we put into street safety improvements now will pay off in fewer crashes and a higher quality of life long-term.

I don’t see a need to significantly increase that $214 million. Instead, we need to use it more efficiently. I’d prioritize within the existing Public Safety budget to ensure our police dedicate enough resources to traffic enforcement, since speeding and reckless driving are public safety threats too. That could mean assigning more officers or units specifically to traffic calming and crosswalk enforcement, and giving them clear directives to crack down on the most dangerous driving behaviors. I also support supplementing police enforcement with smart solutions like automated speed cameras. These have been proven to reduce speeding dramatically. The bottom line is we have to hold drivers accountable to the law, and I’ll make sure our public safety strategy treats traffic violence with the seriousness it deserves, even if we redirect some funds within that big budget to do so.

Yes, absolutely. Many of our streets need a top-to-bottom redesign to put safety first – with things like protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and better crosswalks. Citywide, I’d start with the corridors that we know have the worst crash histories. For example, John F. Kennedy Boulevard stands out as one of the most dangerous roads in Hudson County, with an awful record of pedestrian fatalities over the years. I’d work with the county to calm traffic on JFK.

Another priority is Summit Avenue in the Heights. I support redesigning Summit with protected bike lanes and safer intersections, especially since there are schools and parks along it.

A third example is Martin Luther King Drive/Ocean Avenue in Greenville, where a lot of families walk and traffic can be chaotic. Those streets could benefit from wider sidewalks, crosswalk upgrades, and traffic calming to protect pedestrians.

Overall, I’m committed to bringing safe design to every ward, focusing first on these busy corridors that too often have been built for speeding cars rather than people’s safety.

Converting Summit and Baldwin into a one-way pair so we can add protected bike lanes makes a lot of sense; it would calm traffic and create a safe north-south bike route through the Heights. I’m fully behind using the Baldwin/Summit one-way plan to give pedestrians and cyclists more protection, while still moving traffic efficiently. It’s a smart way to use those federal dollars to save lives and knit our neighborhoods together with safer streets.

The key is to give e-bike and scooter riders a safe space in the street, so they don’t feel the need to use the sidewalk in the first place. That means creating protected bike lanes and dedicated micro-mobility lanes where possible, physically separated from both cars and pedestrians. Alongside that, I’d implement clear rules and signage. For example, a city ordinance reiterating that e-bikes and scooters are not allowed on sidewalks, with possible fines for violations. We can back that up with targeted enforcement in areas where sidewalk riding is a big issue (like busy commercial districts), and with public education for riders about safety and courtesy. By expanding bike infrastructure and doing outreach, we can protect our pedestrian spaces while still accommodating those new modes of travel in the roadway where they belong.

Absolutely. The Newark Avenue Pedestrian Plaza is one of Jersey City’s best success stories, and I fully support making it permanent and even expanding it. In the years since Newark Avenue went car-free, it’s attracted more people downtown, helped more businesses open, and created a true destination spot for visitors and residents. I’ve seen families, seniors, and young people all enjoying that space safely without traffic, and it’s become part of our city’s identity. As mayor, I’d make sure we maintain and improve the Pedestrian Plaza (better lighting, seating, etc.) and look for ways to extend its benefits – whether that’s adding more blocks to it or creating similar spaces in other neighborhoods. It’s proven that when you give streets back to people, the community and the economy thrive, so I’m 100% committed to keeping Newark Ave Plaza a permanent fixture.

Yes, I do. Jersey City is dense and community-oriented, and I believe many areas would benefit from their own pedestrian-only street or plaza. One specific opportunity is Central Avenue in the Heights, behind the Burger King parking lot. There’s already a community-driven plan to revitalize Central Avenue, including building a new pedestrian plaza alongside a parking deck. Creating a car-free plaza on Central Ave would give that neighborhood a safe gathering space for shoppers and families, similar to what Newark Ave has done downtown. It would boost the small businesses there by drawing foot traffic and allow for community events in the heart of the Heights. Beyond that, I’d also look at spots in Journal Square (where so many people walk to the PATH) and Bergen-Lafayette (perhaps near Communipaw Avenue) for shared streets or plazas. The rationale is the same: when you carve out space for people instead of cars, you get safer streets, stronger local businesses, and a better quality of life for the neighborhood.

Yes, I’m a big supporter of bringing bus rapid transit elements to Jersey City. We need faster, more reliable buses on key corridors, for example, routes connecting Journal Square to Downtown, the Heights, Greenville, and Bergen-Lafayette. In fact, I’ve proposed a free citywide bus network built around four major routes linking our neighborhoods. To make those buses rapid, I’m absolutely willing to take steps like dedicated bus lanes, transit signal priority, and yes, even removing some street parking or car lanes if that’s what it takes. On a corridor like JFK Boulevard or Montgomery/Communipaw, giving buses their own lane or priority at lights could dramatically cut travel times. I believe we have to prioritize moving people over storing cars – and if that means repurposing some curbside parking for bus lanes, I’m prepared to do it. The payoff will be buses that run faster and more frequently, which helps everyone get around (and can convince more people to leave the car at home).

Yes, I’m completely willing to repurpose some street parking if it means we can create safer and more efficient travel lanes for people. Curb space in a city is valuable; it can often be put to better use as a bus lane, bike lane, or wider sidewalk rather than free car storage. I’ve already proposed a bold plan for a citywide bus network, which would likely involve dedicating parts of the roadway to buses on key corridors. That inevitably means some parking spots would be removed to make room, and I’ve been vocal about supporting that trade-off. I’ve also spoken out against projects that double-down on car infrastructure (like the Turnpike expansion) in favor of investing in transit and bike/ped improvements. So while it can be controversial, I have no problem standing up and saying: yes, on certain streets we will remove parking spaces to add things like protected bike lanes or bus-only lanes, because those changes benefit far more people in the long run. I’ll always be transparent with the community about these decisions, but I won’t shy away from them – I know a parked car isn’t worth more than a human life or a faster commute for hundreds on a bus.

I am absolutely willing to continue and strengthen Jersey City’s commitment to Vision Zero. The goal of eliminating traffic deaths is one I share wholeheartedly. What I’d do differently is inject a greater sense of urgency and accountability into the process. We’re supposed to hit zero by 2026, and while we’ve made progress, we need to pick up the pace. I’d push for more aggressive implementation of the unfinished Vision Zero Action Plan items, like accelerating street redesigns on the high-injury network and expanding traffic calming citywide. I also want to improve transparency – for example, publishing regular Vision Zero report cards so the public can track how we’re doing on reducing crashes and what projects are in the pipeline. Another thing I’d do is focus on equity within Vision Zero: ensuring that our safety efforts prioritize neighborhoods that have historically been neglected. So yes, I will absolutely carry the Vision Zero torch, but I intend to double down on execution and community engagement to actually deliver the results faster.

Generally, I’m against removing safety infrastructure that’s already in place. If we’ve installed protected bike lanes or raised crosswalks, it was because they serve a clear public safety purpose. I’d be very skeptical of any proposal to rip them out. My stance is that we should give these improvements a chance to do their job and use data to judge them. The kind of data I’d look at includes crash statistics (did crashes or injuries go down after the installation?), usage stats (are cyclists or pedestrians using the new infrastructure in significant numbers?), and any changes in things like traffic flow for drivers. I’d also gather community feedback, of course – are most residents and businesses seeing the benefit, or do they have specific complaints we can address by tweaking the design? The default, though, is that once we’ve made a street safer and more people-friendly, we keep it that way. I wouldn’t support tearing out a bike lane or pedestrian plaza unless the evidence overwhelmingly showed a serious unintended consequence that we couldn’t fix by other means.

One idea is a “Safe Streets for All” campaign that personalizes the issue for our residents. For example, we could feature local Jersey City families in short video PSAs talking about why slowing down or yielding in a crosswalk matters to them (“Hi, I’m a mom in Greenville, I need drivers to stop for my kids at the crosswalk”). These could run on social media, CTV, and at bus shelters. I’d also involve our schools in the campaign: imagine a poster contest for students to draw safe driving messages, with the winning art displayed around the city. By engaging kids, we educate parents at the same time. The campaign would also include workshops or safety fairs in each ward, possibly in partnership with community groups and our police traffic division, to spread awareness of the rules (like how to make a proper left turn, not block the crosswalk, etc.). The key is making it relatable – not just scolding drivers, but reminding everyone that safe streets are in everyone’s interest. If people see their neighbors and local kids leading the message, it hits closer to home and can start shifting the culture.

It’s all about balancing speed with listening. I believe we can do thorough community engagement and still move quickly on lifesaving fixes – the two aren’t mutually exclusive. My approach would be to engage early and often: before we redesign a street, we’d be out in the community with meetings, walking tours, and surveys to gather input and understand local concerns. By bringing neighbors in at the planning stage, you get buy-in and often improve the design with their feedback. At the same time, I’d set clear timelines so that engagement doesn’t turn into an excuse for endless delay. For example, we might say: “We’ll have three public workshops on this project over the next two months, then construction begins in month three.” Throughout, I’d communicate the why – explaining that these measures are about preventing tragedies and that doing nothing is not an option. In my experience, even skeptics often come around when they feel heard and when you show them data or examples of success elsewhere. So we’ll integrate community voices into the design (maybe adjusting a bike lane location or adding a loading zone for a business based on input), but we’ll keep our eyes on the prize of safer streets. And once a plan is ready, I’ll be prepared to implement it decisively, with the community knowing they had a hand in shaping it.

I find the most effective engagement strategies are the ones that meet people where they are: multilingual outreach at town halls, PTA meetings, farmer’s markets, and online tools. I also like demonstration projects, like a temporary curb extension or bike lane, so people can see and react in real time. I won’t be shy about standing up for what’s right; my role is to lead on lifesaving changes, even if it’s controversial, while still listening and making reasonable adjustments. As Board of Education President I fought to eliminate lunch debt and secure fair funding, engaging the community through forums and social media but never wavering from what I knew was right. I’ll bring that same approach to safe streets: honest dialogue, openness to ideas, but firm commitment to protecting lives.

As a former Board of Education member, this issue hits home for me. To give kids safe routes to school, I’d start with basics: more crossing guards, better crosswalks and signage, and strictly enforced school zone speed limits. I also want to pilot “school streets,” closing the block in front of schools like P.S. 28 or P.S. 5 during drop-off and pick-up so kids can arrive without cars speeding by. Working with principals and parents, we’d use cones, signage, and volunteers to manage these closures and promote walking school buses and bike-to-school days. The goal is to make walking or biking to school safe and normal, even if it means inconveniencing drivers for a few minutes.

Safe streets are directly tied to our climate and public health goals – a win-win on both fronts. If we make it safe to walk and bike, more people will choose those modes over driving, cutting carbon emissions and pollution. That means cleaner air for our neighborhoods and healthier residents, since walking and biking naturally build activity into daily life. And the most immediate benefit is fewer injuries and deaths from traffic crashes. Safe streets policy is climate policy and public health policy – by designing a city where it’s easy to leave the car at home, we get cleaner air, safer roads, and healthier people.
